paras: The threatened lynching of Henry Hunt took place in Los Angeles, California, in January 1881, when crowds threatened to take Hunt, accused of murdering ex-policeman George W. Gillis, from the jail and hang him. Officers and armed citizens guarded the jail, and Hunt was later tried and sentenced to life in prison. The episode became known across the country through an anecdote of a mob dispersed by a proposal to take up a collection for the dead officer's widow and orphans.

On the night of January 11, 1881, at El Monte, a man described as a robber and "desperado" shot ex-policeman George Gillis through the abdomen and wounded a resident named Tinker before escaping into the brush. Gillis died of the wound, and Henry Hunt was charged with his murder. According to a Los Angeles dispatch of January 14, a large crowd at Santa Ana had made "loud threats" of lynching the night before, and officers took Hunt out by a back door and brought him to Los Angeles.

On January 14, rumors spread of a plan to take Hunt from the authorities and hang him, and the Sheriff summoned a posse of citizens to guard the jail, joined by the volunteer Los Angeles Guards. The same dispatch found the surrounding streets full of people but "little or no excitement" and judged the threat unlikely to be carried out. A second dispatch reported that as Hunt was taken back to the jail from Justice Adams's court, a man in the crowd with a rope cried "Let's hang him" and was arrested by the Sheriff, and another who cried "hemp" was "squelched."

A later account, first found in the Phoenix Herald on January 28, said that Col. Godfrey addressed the crowd that "wanted to lynch Hunt" and proposed a collection for the widow and orphans of the dead officer, with Joe Manning to gather it. In the fullest version, printed in the Alexandria Gazette, a mob at the City Prison cried "Lynch the cursed scoundrel!", Sheriff Rowland called two hundred citizens to his aid, and the crowd was expected to act at midnight. After Godfrey's speech, that account said, the crowd dissolved until "hardly more than a corporal's guard remained."

Hunt's preliminary examination began before Justice Adams on January 17, when a large crowd filled Spring street and followed him into the courtroom. At his trial before Judge Sepulveda in March, Hunt testified that he fired a single shot because he believed Gillis was reaching for a pistol. The jury convicted him, a new trial was denied on April 11, and he was sentenced to the State's Prison for life. In November 1881 the state Supreme Court affirmed the judgment, rejecting a claim that a juror had been prejudiced against him.

Nevada papers carried the January 14 Los Angeles dispatches the next day, the Eureka Daily Sentinel under the head "Hunt, the Murderer, Nearly Lynched." The collection anecdote then traveled widely, from the Phoenix Herald in January to the Alexandria Gazette in February and the Weekly Clarion of Jackson, Mississippi, and the South Kentuckian in March. Under heads such as "The Ruling Passion" and "A Shrewd Sheriff," these papers presented the story as a joke about would-be lynchers unwilling to pay, and called Hunt "the murderer" throughout. None of the articles found mentions the race of Hunt or Gillis, and no Black-press coverage from this period is available.

The versions differ on who spoke: the Phoenix Herald and the Alexandria Gazette name Col. Godfrey, while the Weekly Clarion credits the Sheriff, standing on a barrel, and the South Kentuckian an unnamed "California Sheriff." They also differ on the crowd: the Weekly Clarion gave "several thousand" and the Gazette an implacable mob surging against the prison, while the contemporaneous dispatch reported little excitement. The January 14 dispatch is the more direct evidence of the scene, since the dramatic details appear only in the later, widely copied anecdote.

bases: Crowds at Santa Ana and at the Los Angeles jail threatened to hang Hunt, accused of murdering an ex-policeman, and were held off and dispersed without a killing (A2, A3, A8).

A crowd threatened to take Hunt from the jail and hang him for the killing of Gillis, but he was not harmed and was later tried and sentenced to life (A2, A8, A18); no one was killed, so it was a threatened, not a completed, lynching.

Two separate Jan. 14 Los Angeles dispatches report lynching threats against Hunt at the jail (A2, A3), and a separately circulated anecdote reports a mob there dispersed by a collection speech (A6, A8), though its details vary between versions (A11, A13).
